name: Jade Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The farm's a mix: a hundred and twenty dairy cows, two thousand free-range hens and about forty hectares of potatoes. Two years ago the Davies family put in two milking robots, and I'm the one who looks after them, so my day starts with the overnight alerts on my phone. A cow that didn't come in to be milked, a teat cup that keeps slipping, that sort of thing. Then I'm out with the hens, and in autumn it's potato harvest, which is just mud and noise for six weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving things. Every morning there's a puzzle, why's number 412 giving less milk, is it her feet or the feed. What wears me out is being on call, because the robots ring me at two in the morning if a cow kicks the arm off. They're brilliant, but they don't know what time it is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an assistant to check feed rations against the milk records, write up the egg grading reports and draft emails to the vet. Owen Davies, the boss, calls me the farm's brain, which is flattering and also means nobody else bothers to learn it. I'm single, I live in a cottage on the farm, and I rent out a little flat I bought in town, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I always told people, the tools are good for specific jobs and the rest is marketing. I'd post a photo of the milking robot with a caption like still waiting for it to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes much, and the job's good. I'd keep using the assistant for the rations and reports, because it saves me hours a week. I'd probably get a bit restless, though, because I like new things to figure out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and maybe push Owen to try the egg-counting cameras I've read about. I'd keep paying down the flat's mortgage faster with the rent money. Maybe take a proper holiday, which I haven't done in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little itch for something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody else bothers to learn the systems. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If I broke my leg tomorrow, the robots would be stuck with Owen phoning the dealer every hour. I keep meaning to teach Dylan, the other worker, but he's happier with the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the holiday be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere with no cows and good mobile signal, so I can still check the alerts. Which I know defeats the point. My sister says I'm married to the robots.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are good for specific jobs and the rest is marketing, which is what I always told people. I'd post a photo of our milking robot captioned still waiting for it to take over.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, and the job's good, so I'd keep using AI for rations and reports. I'd probably get a bit restless, because I like new things to figure out.
S0.do: Keeps working and pushes her boss to try egg-counting cameras. Pays down the mortgage on her rented-out flat faster and takes her first proper holiday in three years.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little itch for something new.
S0.quote: If I broke my leg tomorrow, the robots would be stuck with Owen phoning the dealer every hour.
S0.fieldNote: Jade already runs the farm's milking robots and uses AI every day, so the plateau barely touches her. Her quiet worry is being the only person who understands the systems. She'd still check alerts on holiday, and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt will do fine and farms that don't will struggle, same as always. I'd say it to the young farmers' group, where I sometimes give talks about the robots. I'd keep it practical, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. Someone who understands the robots and the cows is worth more, not less, in a world like that. The dealer has asked me twice whether I'd come and work for them, and in this version I'd probably say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Owen to bring in the egg cameras and a robot feed-pusher within the year, and I'd set them up. I'd start doing paid weekend visits to help other farms with their robots, maybe one or two a month. And I'd teach Dylan the basics so I can actually go on holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the weekend visits bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred a month to start, if the dealer doesn't mind. Farms round here would rather pay someone who's milked cows than a technician who's only seen them on a screen. I'd put all of it into the flat or savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dylan, probably, if the tractor work gets automated. He's thirty and he loves his tractor more than most people love their dog. I'd want Owen to keep him on for the potatoes, because they still need someone with a feel for when the ground's right.

S1.say: I'd say farms that adapt will do fine and farms that don't will struggle, same as always. I'd keep it practical when I talk to the young farmers' group.
S1.think: Privately this is good for me, because someone who understands both robots and cows becomes worth more. The machinery dealer has asked me twice to work for them, and here I'd probably say yes.
S1.do: Pushes her boss to bring in egg cameras and a robot feed-pusher within the year and sets them up herself. Starts paid weekend visits to help other farms with their robots and teaches her colleague the basics.
S1.quote: He's thirty and he loves his tractor more than most people love their dog.
S1.fieldNote: This scenario reads as an opportunity for her, and she has already been headhunted by the dealer. She thought of her colleague Dylan when asked and argued for keeping him on. Her side income idea is concrete and modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and anyone saying it's fine is lying. I'd also say the people who understand the machines have a job for now, so learn them. I'd probably post a long thread about what's happening on real farms, because people would want to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay for a year or two. I'd be the last one on the farm, babysitting the robots. But if the AI can fix its own robots, then I'm just the person who unlocks the shed. I've got the flat and savings, so I wouldn't be on the street, but I'd lose the thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy shares in a couple of the robot and AI companies straight away, because if they're taking the work, I want a slice. I'd take the dealer job if it was still going and learn every new system they sold. And I'd look at turning the flat into a holiday let for more income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More restless than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying shares in the companies taking the jobs a bit strange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm not sentimental about it. Owen bought the milking robots to save on wages, and I helped him choose them. If it's going to happen anyway, I'd rather own a bit of it than just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is about one good bet. I can't retrain properly, I can only grab what's in front of me, the dealer job and the shares. With longer, I'd do something more thought through.

S2.say: I'd say this is huge and anyone claiming it's fine is lying, but people who understand the machines have a job for now. I'd post a long thread about what's really happening on farms.
S2.think: I'd be okay for a year or two as the last one babysitting the robots, until the AI can fix them itself. With my flat and savings I wouldn't be on the street, but I'd lose the thing I'm good at.
S2.do: Buys shares in a couple of robot and AI companies straight away and takes the dealer job if it's still open. Learns every new system they sell and looks at turning her flat into a holiday let.
S2.quote: If the AI can fix its own robots, then I'm just the person who unlocks the shed.
S2.fieldNote: She's unsentimental about owning a piece of the companies doing the replacing, and pointed out she already helped her boss automate. Her fear is losing meaningful work rather than income. Two years, to her, is time for one good bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're not lazy about it. I'd do talks for the young farmers on what skills still matter. And I'd say the government should help with training costs, because not everyone has savings like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to make two moves, not one. I'd go to the dealer first, then set up something of my own before 2031. I don't know what that something is yet, but I'd have time to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd take the dealer job and do their advanced training on the new robots. I'd keep the flat and add a second one if I could, as a steady income that doesn't depend on any job. And I'd start testing ideas, like a farm open day business with Owen, where people come to see how food is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an open day business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots do everything, people will still want to see where their milk comes from, and they'll want a person to tell them. Kids from the school come every spring and go mad for the calves. That doesn't stop being worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be buying a second flat in an uncertain world. What makes that feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still need somewhere to live, robots or not. It's not exciting, but it's the bit of my plan that would work even if every other bit failed. My dad taught me that, he's an accountant and he's boring and he's always right.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're not lazy about it, and I'd tell young farmers which skills still matter. The government should help with training costs, because not everyone has savings.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make two moves, first to the machinery dealer and then into something of my own before 2031. I don't know what that something is yet, but I'd have time to find out.
S3.do: Takes the dealer job and its advanced robot training in the first year. Keeps her flat and tries to buy a second one for steady rental income, and tests a farm open day business with her boss.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, because she likes having a plan.
S3.quote: My dad taught me that, he's an accountant and he's boring and he's always right.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she makes a two-step plan and adds property as a safety net. Her open day idea comes from watching school groups with the calves. She believes the human role left will be showing and explaining, not producing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads, and the farms that waste it only have themselves to blame. That might sound harsh, but I'd say it kindly. I'd also be the one offering to help them get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I think I'd do really well, to be honest. I'd have time to build a business, own a couple of flats, and be the person farms call when they need robots set up properly. The worry is more about what happens after 2036, when even that's done by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the Davies farm a couple more years to learn everything, then go to the dealer, then start my own farm robot service by about thirty-two. I'd keep buying property slowly. And I'd do the open day business on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the worry is what happens after 2036. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm with nobody on it. Owen's retired, Dylan's gone, the cows walk into the robot on their own. I'd be fine for money, I think, but I'd want there to still be a reason to get up at half five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does more warning time change who you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years, I'd worry less for Dylan because he'd have time to find something. With two, I'd worry about him a lot, because he'd never move until someone made him.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is loads, and farms that waste it only have themselves to blame, though I'd say it kindly. I'd also be the one offering to help them get started.
S4.think: With ten years I think I'd do really well, with a business and a couple of flats. My worry is what happens after 2036, when even that's done by machines.
S4.do: Stays at the farm a couple more years to learn everything, then joins the machinery dealer, then starts her own farm robot service by about thirty-two. Keeps buying property slowly and runs farm open days on the side.
S4.feel: Calm, like she can see the road ahead.
S4.quote: I'd want there to still be a reason to get up at half five.
S4.fieldNote: She expects to do well financially and her real concern is meaning, not money. More time made her worry less for her colleague Dylan, which she noticed herself. Her plan is staged, practical and fully self-funded.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not because I'd be broke. It's because I'd go from being good at something to being someone who unlocks a shed. What would help is people like me being involved in how the robots are brought onto farms, and some help for people like Dylan who won't move until they're pushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what the cows would think. That sounds daft, but the robots changed how the herd behaves. They come in when they want now, they're calmer. I'm not sure people would be, if their lives got rearranged by a machine that suits someone else's timetable.

headlineQuote: I'd go from being good at something to being someone who unlocks a shed.
portrait: Jade Patel, 27, looks after the milking robots on a mixed dairy, egg and potato farm, uses AI every day and owns a small flat in town that she rents out. She's single, brisk and unsentimental, and the machinery dealer has already tried to hire her. The AI Plateau leaves her restless, Steady Disruption looks like an opportunity, and AGI by 2028 makes her uneasy enough to buy shares in the companies doing the replacing. With five or ten years she plans a move to the dealer, her own robot service and more property, and her deepest worry is losing a reason to get up in the morning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd go from being good at something to being someone who unlocks a shed.
whatWouldHelp: Having farmworkers like her involved in how robots are brought onto farms, and help for colleagues like Dylan who won't move until they're pushed.
